To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the CBF response to hypoxia is closely related to CMRO2, and that the CBF autoregulatory response is not altered by the level of anesthesia.
the CBF response to hypoxia is closely tied to CM RO2 and that the autoregulatory response is not impaired by barbiturate coma.
the CBF response to isocapneic hypoxic hypoxemia is attenuated during pentobarbalt coma, but only as much as CMRO2 is reduced.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of altered cerebral oxygen consumption on the cerebrovascular responses to hypoxemia and hypotension.
the mechanisms of cerebral blood flow control.
the mechanisms of cerebral vascular autoregulation, and in particular with the role of metabolic factors in determining the autoregulatory response.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
in sheep, the CBF response to hypoxia and the autoregulation of CBF are maintained when CMRO2 is reduced by 50%.
the cerebral circulation is not autoregulated in sheep.

(1) the cerebrovascular response to hypoxia and autoregulation of CBF are closely tied to the base-line CMRO; and (2) barbiturate coma does not impair the cerebrovascular autonomic responses to either hypoxia or hypotension.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, although there is a direct relationship between CMRO2 and base-line CBF, the CBF response to changes in CMRO2 is not linear.
the cerebral vasculature is exquisitely sensitive to changes in CMRO2 and is capable of maintaining a constant CaO2 X CBR even when CMRO2 is reduced by 50%.

The main takeaway from our work is that
CBF responses are closely linked to the metabolic rate of the brain.
the brain is very good at maintaining its oxygenation during hypoxia.
the cerebrovascular system responds appropriately to the demands placed on it by the brain.
